## Simple explanation

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is a standard way for an AI application to
connect to external capabilities and information. Instead of building a
different integration for every tool, an application can communicate with
MCP-compatible servers through a shared protocol.

## Technical explanation

MCP defines client-server interactions and capability types, including
resources, prompts, and tools. A host application creates clients that
connect to servers; servers expose capabilities for clients to discover and
use. The protocol describes message exchange and lifecycle behavior, while
authentication, authorization, deployment, and user approval depend on the
implementation and environment.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Standardized integrations can make tools and data sources reusable across
compatible AI applications. MCP also creates a security boundary: exposed
tools may have side effects or access sensitive data, so applications should
limit permissions, validate inputs, and make consequential actions visible
to users.

## How it works

An MCP client establishes a connection to a server and negotiates supported
capabilities. The client can then list or invoke tools, read resources, or
retrieve prompts according to the protocol. The host application decides
which capabilities to expose to a model and how to handle approvals and
results.

## Practical example

A development assistant can connect to an MCP server that provides
read-only access to project documentation. When a user asks about an API, the
assistant can discover and retrieve relevant documentation through the server
rather than embedding the entire document set in its prompt.

## Common misconceptions

- MCP is a connectivity protocol, not an AI model or an agent by itself.
- A compatible server is not automatically safe; capabilities and permissions still need review.
- MCP does not guarantee that a model will use a tool correctly or that returned data is trustworthy.
